newsitem.title: USA: Balmy fall boosts big U.S. crops, eases food fear.
newsitem.headline: Balmy fall boosts big U.S. crops, eases food fear.

text.p: Perfect fall weather sharply boosted the size of near-record U.S. corn and soybean crops, easing fears of a surge in food prices, the Agriculture Department said on Tuesday.

It forecast a corn crop of 9.27 billion bushels, the third largest on record and 3 percent above its October estimate. The soybean harvest was pegged at 2.40 billion bushels, the second largest crop ever and 2 percent bigger than thought last month.
Stockpiles would remain tight, however, making another large crop vital in 1997.

Large U.S. crops would hold food price inflation to four percent or so, analysts said, far lower than was projected in mid-summer, when the outlook was worrisome and grain prices soared. Crops were retarded by a wet spring and cool summer but were blessed by warm, sunny weather in the final weeks.
"It just got to the edge of being serious and then the crops got good," said private consultant John Schnittker. "It was an amazing fall."

Based on Nov. 1 conditions, the Agriculture Department raised its forecast of corn yields in all major states and said the crop would average 126.5 bushels an acre nationwide, up 3.5 bushels in a month. Soybean yields were up 0.9 bushels an acre for a projected 37.9 due to "nearly ideal weather."
Heavy demand at home and abroad was forecast to consume most of the gargantuan output, leaving little cushion against a shortfall next year.
About 210 million bushels of soybeans would be on hand when the 1997 harvest began, the department said, and 1.1 billion bushels of corn.
The corn "carry over" would be more than twice as large as this fall but still 30 percent lower than 1995's level.
Cotton output was estimated at 18.59 million bales, third highest ever and up 400,000 bales from October due to improved yields, now forecast for 698 pounds per acre. There are 480 pounds in a bale.
